title: Gilgamesh: The King's Dream
subtitle: A tyrant so strong the gods must build him a match

What do the gods create in answer?

dream.work: An Old Babylonian Version of the Gilgamesh Epic
dream.author: Anonymous
dream.translator: Morris Jastrow and Albert T. Clay
dream.locator: Pennsylvania Tablet · Column I; Pennsylvania Tablet · Column I, normalized characters 841-1231
dream.excerpt: My likeness I have seen in the streets [Of Erech] of the plazas. An axe was brandished, and They gathered about him; And the axe made him angry. I saw him and I rejoiced, I loved him as a woman, I embraced him. I took him and regarded him As my brother." The mother of Gish, who knows all things, [Spoke to Gish]: ["O Gish, the man whom thou sawest,] [Whom thou didst embrace like a woman].
dream.note: Verbatim translation from the named Old Babylonian tablet witness in this edited edition. Brackets and question marks signal textual restoration or uncertainty.

narrativeBlocks.title: Two-thirds god, all problem
narrativeBlocks.body: Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, is part divine and entirely too much: he exhausts his own people — young men conscripted for his endless games, brides claimed before their weddings. The city prays for relief.

narrativeBlocks.title: The gods' answer is not punishment
narrativeBlocks.body: Instead of destroying him, the gods make a COUNTERWEIGHT: a wild man named Enkidu, shaped from clay, running with the herds on the steppe — Gilgamesh's equal in strength.

narrativeBlocks.title: A dream foretells him
narrativeBlocks.body: Gilgamesh dreams of a meteor — or an axe — that he loves like a wife. His mother Ninsun reads it: a companion is coming who will be as strong as you and will save your life.

narrativeBlocks.title: The epic's real engine
narrativeBlocks.body: The story that follows is not about a tyrant being punished — it is about the first friendship in world literature, and what it costs. Everything in Gilgamesh turns on the bond formed next.

narrativeBlocks.title: Oldest epic, newest problem
narrativeBlocks.body: This is the oldest surviving epic (c. 2100 BCE) — and its opening question is still ours: what do you do with a leader no one can stop? The gods' answer: give him an equal, not an enemy.

quiz.prompt: Why do the people of Uruk cry out to the gods?

choices.text: Gilgamesh is an unbearable tyrant — exhausting the city with conscription and claiming brides

quiz.explanation: He's too strong and too much — the problem is his unchecked greatness, not an external enemy.

quiz.prompt: What do the gods create in answer?

choices.text: Enkidu — a wild man of the steppe, Gilgamesh's equal and destined companion
A second king to depose him
A flood to humble the city

quiz.explanation: The gods' fix is a counterweight, not a punishment — the first friendship begins.
